method: Rebuild from primary text. Health & Safety Code chapter 6.6 (§§25249.5 to 25249.14) was fetched in full from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and read section by section. The Article 6 warning regulations could NOT be read — see gaps. Construing case law was located through CourtListener. Assertions describe the REBUILT body.
queries: Cal. Health & Safety Code ch. 6.6 full text (leginfo)
"25249.6" Proposition 65 clear and reasonable warning knowingly intentionally
Prop 65 fewer than 10 employees person in the course of doing business

assertions.text: no person in the course of doing business shall knowingly and intentionally expose an individual to a listed chemical without first giving clear and reasonable warning
assertions.note: §25249.6, verbatim. The previous body said goods 'may require a Proposition 65 warning where they expose a person to a listed chemical' and had no knowledge or intent element at all.

assertions.text: 'person in the course of doing business' does not include a person employing fewer than 10 employees
assertions.note: §25249.11(b), verbatim, and stated by the Court of Appeal in Environmental Law Foundation v. Wykle Research. This is the qualifier the previous body's own defect list called the single most consequential one in the statute, and the previous body stated the duty with no threshold.

assertions.text: the exemption is personal to the exempt party and relieves no one else in the chain
assertions.note: Follows from §25249.11(b), which defines who is covered rather than exempting a product, and from Wykle's observation that because dentists with fewer than ten employees are not subject to the mandate, a manufacturer's transmission of warnings to dentists does not ensure the warning reaches patients.

assertions.text: constructive knowledge suffices for the 'knowingly and intentionally' element
assertions.note: Lee v. Amazon.com, quoted below. This is a construction that changes what the words mean and it runs against the reader: a seller who did not look is not therefore safe. Nothing in the previous body suggested it.

assertions.text: a warning that departs from the safe-harbour regulations loses the safe harbour rather than being void
assertions.note: The statutory standard in §25249.6 is a 'clear and reasonable warning'; §25249.11(f) contemplates general warning methods 'provided that the warning accomplished is clear and reasonable'. Nothing in chapter 6.6 makes a non-conforming warning a nullity. The previous body's 'a warning that is present but non-conforming is treated as no warning at all' overstated it. The regulations themselves could not be read — see gaps.

assertions.text: primary responsibility for a consumer product exposure rests upstream rather than on the retail seller
assertions.note: §25249.11(f) directs that 'regulations implementing Section 25249.6 shall to the extent practicable place the obligation to provide any warning materials such as labels on the producer or packager rather than on the retail seller'. 27 C.C.R. §25600.2 implements that, and was read ONLY as quoted by the Court of Appeal in Lee v. Amazon.com. Carried in the clause body behind an explicit NOT VERIFIED marker.

assertions.text: three exemptions: federal preemption, exposure within twelve months of listing, and no significant risk on the statutory measure with the burden on the defendant
assertions.note: §25249.10(a)-(c), verbatim, including that 'the burden of showing that an exposure meets the criteria of this subdivision shall be on the defendant'.

assertions.text: enforcement, the 60-day notice with certificate of merit, and the diligent-prosecution bar
assertions.note: §25249.7(c)-(d). The certificate of merit requirement in §25249.7(d)(1) applies where the notice alleges a §25249.6 violation, which is this clause's subject.

assertions.text: the civil penalty is up to $2,500 per day for each violation, assessed against seven factors
assertions.note: §25249.7(b)(1)-(2). The seven factors include 'Whether the violator took good faith measures to comply with this chapter and the time these measures were taken', which is the statutory hook for a documented compliance programme.

priorDefects: omitted: the knowledge and intent element in §25249.6 entirely.
overstated: 'a warning that is present but non-conforming is treated as no warning at all'.
omitted: that constructive knowledge suffices (Lee v. Amazon.com).
omitted: the $2,500-per-day penalty figure and the seven statutory factors.
omitted: the certificate of merit and the diligent-prosecution bar, which are the two things that make a 60-day notice defensible.

unsupported as stated: 'Enforcement is primarily by private plaintiffs who recover attorney's fees'. Nothing in chapter 6.6 read here provides for a private plaintiff's fee recovery; §25249.7 says nothing about fees. Private Prop 65 fee awards are generally taken under Code of Civil Procedure §1021.5, which was not read. The rebuilt body describes who may enforce and does not repeat the fee claim.
gaps: The Article 6 safe-harbour regulations — 27 C.C.R. §25600 and following, including §25600.2 on allocation of responsibility and the internet-purchase provisions — could not be read from any publisher. govt.westlaw.com, the publisher of the California Code of Regulations, returns HTTP 403 at this environment's egress proxy. oehha.ca.gov and p65warnings.ca.gov, the promulgating agency's own sites, return an Incapsula firewall challenge page rather than the document, on both the regulation index and the direct PDF paths tried. What the clause says about the regulations is carried behind an explicit NOT VERIFIED marker and rests on the Court of Appeal's quotation of §25600.2, which is a court quoting a regulation and not the text.

The clause fires only when industry is ecommerce. Proposition 65 is not an ecommerce statute and a manufacturer or physical retailer with ten or more employees is equally covered. The condition was not changed by this rebuild and it means the clause will not reach parties who need it.
Whether a private plaintiff recovers attorney's fees, and under what provision, was not verified. The previous body asserted it as the reason the statute is enforced at volume.

The internet-purchase placement rules are in Article 6 and were not read, so the instruction to allocate responsibility for placement 'including on the product page' has no verified content behind it.

judicialQuotations.case: Lee v. Amazon.com, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 2022)
judicialQuotations.quote: Interpreting section 25249.6 to require warnings only when a person in the course of doing business has actual knowledge that he or she will expose any individual to a listed chemical would significantly limit the reach of the statute and create incentives to avoid information that might reveal potential sources of exposure.

judicialQuotations.case: Lee v. Amazon.com, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 2022)
judicialQuotations.quote: We see no basis for reading "intentionally" in section 25249.6 as essentially modifying "knowingly" to require a higher level of knowledge than "knowingly" would otherwise convey. As we have said, an actual knowledge requirement would narrow the scope of section 25249.6, contrary to the purpose of Proposition 65.

judicialQuotations.case: Lee v. Amazon.com, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 2022) — quoting 27 C.C.R. §25600.2(e)
judicialQuotations.quote: The retail seller is responsible for providing the warning required by Section 25249.6 of the Act for a consumer product exposure only when . . . [the] retail seller has actual knowledge of the potential consumer product exposure requiring the warning, and there is no manufacturer, producer, packager, importer, supplier, or distributor of the product who: . . . [i]s a "person in the course of doing business" under Section 25249.11(b) of the Act

judicialQuotations.case: Environmental Law Foundation v. Wykle Research, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 2005) 134 Cal.App.4th 60
judicialQuotations.quote: Every dentist is a "person" within the meaning of the statute (Health & Saf. Code, § 25249.11, subd. (a)), but a "person in the course of doing business" does not include one who employs fewer than 10 employees in his or her business (id., subd. (b)). Many dentists therefore may not be subject to the mandate of the statute.
